title: Trump’s Destruction of Iranian Life Is Strengthening the Regime
gist: Nik Kowsar and Alireza Nader argue the U.S.-Israeli campaign against Iranian civilian infrastructure is strengthening the Islamic Republic by letting it pose as national defender, and has opened a reciprocal water-and-power war across the Gulf: a mid-July U.S. strike on the Bonji desalination plant in Jask county cut drinking water to roughly 10,000 people and 20 villages, while Iran has retaliated against Kuwait's power and desalination assets, Bahrain's water and power, and earlier Saudi energy infrastructure. They document how Iran's IRGC engineering arm Khatam al-Anbiya blurred civilian and military infrastructure through decades of dam, metro, water-transfer and tunneling work, making clean targeting effectively impossible.

themes.theme: Civilian targeting is strengthening the regime

insights.claim: Conducting the war as if it were against the entire nation of Iran rather than the regime has let the Islamic Republic portray itself as Iran's national defender rather than its occupier, undercutting the population's ability to overthrow it.
insights.speaker: Nik Kowsar, Alireza Nader
insights.so_what: Regime-change-by-bombing is producing regime consolidation, which extends the expected duration of the conflict and its energy risk premium.
insights.quote: a war that has been devastating to the civilian population has helped the regime to portray itself as Iran’s national defender rather than its occupier
insights.locator: Millions of Iranians despise the Islamic Republic

insights.claim: Millions of Iranians rose against the Islamic Republic only six months ago and thousands were massacred by the regime in January, and some initially supported the war hoping the U.S. and Israel would finish what their uprising started.
insights.speaker: Nik Kowsar, Alireza Nader
insights.so_what: There was a genuine domestic opposition base that the war has now alienated — the loss of that option removes the cheapest path to regime change.
insights.locator: Millions of Iranians despise the Islamic Republic

insights.claim: Trump promised that help was on its way when thousands of unarmed Iranian protesters were massacred in January, but his war has instead created hardship for ordinary people, especially in the southern region abutting the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz.
insights.speaker: Nik Kowsar, Alireza Nader
insights.so_what: The credibility gap between U.S. rhetoric and outcomes reduces the odds any future U.S. appeal to Iranian society gains traction.
insights.quote: Ironically, Trump promised that “help [was] on its way” when thousands of unarmed protesters were massacred in January.
insights.locator: Ironically, Trump promised that

insights.claim: The Islamic Republic has not only survived the war but inflicted significant damage on the U.S. military and rattled the global economy.
insights.speaker: Nik Kowsar, Alireza Nader
insights.so_what: Survival plus economic disruption is a win condition for Tehran — do not model Iranian capitulation as the base case.
insights.locator: The Islamic Republic has managed not only to survive

insights.claim: Destroying civilian infrastructure weakens Iranians' ability to organize, rebuild and pursue political change, because people consumed by the search for water, food, medicine, fuel and shelter have little strength left for democratic mobilization — and authoritarian governments know how to use scarcity and dependence to tighten their grip.
insights.speaker: Nik Kowsar, Alireza Nader
insights.so_what: A general model: infrastructure destruction is anti-democratic in effect, which inverts the stated theory of the campaign.
insights.quote: People consumed by the search for water, food, medicine, fuel, and shelter have little time or strength left for democratic mobilization.
insights.locator: Destroying civilian infrastructure also weakens

themes.theme: Water infrastructure as the new front line

insights.claim: A mid-July U.S. airstrike damaged the desalination facility in Bonji in western Jask county as part of a wider assault on Iran's southern coastal infrastructure, cutting drinking water access for about 10,000 people and leaving 20 villages without supply for days at the height of summer.
insights.speaker: Nik Kowsar, Alireza Nader
insights.so_what: A documented case of desalination assets being struck — establishes precedent that Gulf water infrastructure is now a legitimate military target class.
insights.quote: The damage to the facility resulted in about 10,000 people losing access to drinking water.
insights.locator: A mid-July U.S. airstrike damaged the desalination facility

insights.claim: Water tankers cannot replace a municipal system serving scattered villages, and during extreme heat demand rises just as transportation and storage of water become more difficult.
insights.speaker: Nik Kowsar, Alireza Nader
insights.so_what: Explains why desalination damage compounds nonlinearly in summer — the timing of strikes drives the humanitarian and political outcome.
insights.locator: Tankers can provide temporary relief

insights.claim: Water, electricity, transportation, food and health systems are closely connected, so damage to one can quickly spread to the others while hardened and bunkered military forces continue fighting.
insights.speaker: Nik Kowsar, Alireza Nader
insights.so_what: Infrastructure interdependence means civilian cost scales faster than military effect — the core asymmetry of this targeting strategy.
insights.quote: Such strikes can impose immediate suffering on civilians while leaving hardened and bunkered military forces capable of continuing the war.
insights.locator: Bonji shows why attacking infrastructure

insights.claim: The roads, bridges and railways the U.S. is hitting in southern Iran serve both Iranian troop and weapons movement near the Strait of Hormuz and the civilian transport of food, fuel and medicine, so the strikes cannot be cleanly separated.
insights.speaker: Nik Kowsar, Alireza Nader
insights.so_what: Dual-use transport targeting guarantees civilian harm claims and legal exposure regardless of intent.
insights.locator: The United States claims it is targeting military sites

themes.theme: GCC retaliation vector and regional water risk

insights.claim: Iran has sent a clear message through attacks on U.S. and allied bases across the Persian Gulf that it will destroy energy and water infrastructure necessary to the survival of tens of millions in the Gulf Cooperation Council states if its own critical infrastructure is targeted.
insights.speaker: Nik Kowsar, Alireza Nader
insights.so_what: Explicit reciprocal-deterrence doctrine on water and power puts GCC utilities, petrochemical and desalination assets in the direct risk path.
insights.quote: It will destroy energy and water infrastructure necessary to the survival of tens of millions of people in the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) states if Iran’s critical infrastructure is targeted.
insights.locator: The Islamic Republic has managed not only to survive

insights.claim: Iran attacked Kuwait's power and water infrastructure, shutting down several generating units and starting a fire at a desalination facility, and has also struck water and power facilities in Bahrain and earlier Saudi Arabia's energy infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Nik Kowsar, Alireza Nader
insights.so_what: Named-country strike record on utilities — a direct input to Gulf sovereign risk, insurance pricing and regional power-project underwriting.
insights.locator: Alarmingly, the attack on Iran's infrastructure has been met

insights.claim: GCC states rely heavily on desalination plants for their water needs and Iran has demonstrated the capability to damage or destroy much of the GCC's desalination and water infrastructure, which in one of the hottest and driest regions on Earth is a lifeline.
insights.speaker: Nik Kowsar, Alireza Nader
insights.so_what: Existential single-point-of-failure exposure for Gulf economies — the strongest argument for GCC states to press Washington toward de-escalation.
insights.locator: The damage in Kuwait may not produce widespread water cuts yet

insights.claim: If the cycle continues, attacks on water and power will become a normal form of retaliation across a region that cannot survive them.
insights.speaker: Nik Kowsar, Alireza Nader
insights.so_what: Normalization of utility strikes would permanently raise the risk discount on Gulf infrastructure and industrial capacity.
insights.quote: Otherwise, attacks on water and power will become a normal form of retaliation across a region that cannot survive them.
insights.locator: Otherwise, attacks on water and power

insights.claim: Iran developed its tunneling capacity through ostensibly civilian work, acquiring tunnel-boring machines and excavation expertise over decades via metro systems, mines, dams and inter-basin water-transfer projects.
insights.speaker: Nik Kowsar, Alireza Nader
insights.so_what: Dual-use capability acquisition through civil megaprojects is a proliferation channel export-control regimes largely miss.
insights.locator: The regime developed much of its tunneling capacity

insights.claim: Khatam al-Anbiya Construction Headquarters, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' engineering arm, and companies it owns or controls have played major roles across Iran's dam, water-transfer, tunneling, pipeline and transportation projects, letting expertise and equipment move between civilian, nuclear and military sectors.
insights.speaker: Nik Kowsar, Alireza Nader
insights.so_what: Names the specific institutional node where sanctions and targeting decisions have maximum leverage and maximum civilian spillover.
insights.locator: Khatam al-Anbiya Construction Headquarters

insights.claim: Independent Iranian water-management engineers familiar with major excavation projects told the authors they suspect equipment and tunnels officially associated with mining, water-transfer and metro projects may also have been used to build military and nuclear facilities, with sources last year describing links between water projects and Fordow.
insights.speaker: Nik Kowsar, Alireza Nader
insights.so_what: Original sourcing on civil-nuclear equipment overlap — a template for tracing covert construction through public infrastructure procurement.
insights.locator: Several independent Iranian water-management engineers

insights.claim: Iran's nuclear facilities depend on water, electricity, roads, communications and specialized supply chains that also serve nearby cities, farms and industries; in 2006 the Isfahan governor's office reported that 6.5 million cubic meters of water had been transferred to a nuclear facility.
insights.speaker: Nik Kowsar, Alireza Nader
insights.so_what: Quantified civil-nuclear water coupling — evidence that striking nuclear support infrastructure necessarily hits civilian systems.
insights.quote: In 2006, the Isfahan governor’s office reported that 6.5 million cubic meters of water had been transferred to a nuclear facility.
insights.locator: Iran's nuclear facilities do not exist in isolation

insights.claim: The regime has spent decades moving its most sensitive nuclear and military assets underground — Fordow beneath a mountain, newer facilities like Pickaxe Mountain excavated around Natanz — and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has implied that tunnels and underground facilities are regularly used by high-level decision-makers.
insights.speaker: Nik Kowsar, Alireza Nader
insights.so_what: Hardened leadership and program survivability means decapitation and obliteration claims should be heavily discounted.
insights.locator: The regime has spent decades moving its most sensitive

insights.claim: Damage to an operating reactor, chemical-processing plant, cooling system or nuclear-material storage site could release radioactive or toxic substances, and the IAEA has repeatedly warned that attacks on nuclear facilities undermine nuclear safety with consequences beyond Iran's borders.
insights.speaker: Nik Kowsar, Alireza Nader
insights.so_what: A cross-border radiological event is the low-probability, high-impact tail that would reprice regional aviation, shipping and Gulf assets instantly.
insights.locator: Attacking nuclear-related infrastructure directly creates huge risks

insights.claim: Even without a radioactive release, war interrupts inspections, destroys monitoring equipment and scatters records, making nuclear material harder to account for, while bombing may delay parts of the program without eliminating the expertise or political incentive behind it.
insights.speaker: Nik Kowsar, Alireza Nader
insights.so_what: Loss of verification is the durable cost of the campaign — it raises long-run proliferation uncertainty even if strikes appear successful.
insights.quote: Technical knowledge survives bombing. Power grids, hospitals, bridges, water-treatment plants, and public trust are much harder to rebuild.
insights.locator: Even when there is no release of radioactive material

insights.claim: Bombing may persuade Iranian leaders that future nuclear facilities must be built deeper underground, spread across more locations and hidden more carefully from inspectors.
insights.speaker: Nik Kowsar, Alireza Nader
insights.so_what: The campaign likely worsens long-run detectability — a counterproductive outcome that argues against strikes as a nonproliferation tool.
insights.locator: Even when there is no release of radioactive material

themes.theme: Policy prescription and the distinction that matters

insights.claim: The authors call on Washington to abandon forcing regime change by military action, avoid targeting drinking water, sanitation, health and civilian energy systems, and ensure sanctions and operations do not obstruct emergency repairs or delivery of medicines, water-treatment chemicals, spare parts and generators.
insights.speaker: Nik Kowsar, Alireza Nader
insights.so_what: A concrete list of policy carve-outs to watch for as an early signal that Washington is moderating the campaign.
insights.locator: Washington should abandon trying to force regime change

insights.claim: The regime has repeatedly shown itself willing to pursue a scorched-earth strategy, sacrificing the country's infrastructure and its people to preserve its own power, which makes infrastructure escalation especially dangerous.
insights.speaker: Nik Kowsar, Alireza Nader
insights.so_what: An adversary indifferent to national cost cannot be coerced through national cost — the central flaw in the pressure theory.
insights.locator: The danger is even greater when confronting a regime

insights.claim: Weakening a government and breaking a country are not the same thing: regimes can fall and armies withdraw, but poisoned aquifers, collapsed power grids and destroyed water systems can condemn civilians to displacement, disease and poverty for generations.
insights.speaker: Nik Kowsar, Alireza Nader
insights.so_what: The framing to apply when assessing reconstruction timelines and long-run country risk after any infrastructure-targeting campaign.
insights.quote: Weakening a government and breaking a country are not the same thing.
insights.locator: The danger is even greater when confronting a regime

insights.claim: Targeting critical infrastructure means devastation for tens of millions of Iranians in a country already on the brink of environmental collapse, putting the entire Persian Gulf region's economy and environment in grave danger.
insights.speaker: Nik Kowsar, Alireza Nader
insights.so_what: Pre-existing Iranian environmental fragility multiplies war damage — relevant to migration, food and regional stability forecasts.
insights.locator: The U.S. and Israeli war against Iran has intensified again
